# Raw bindings

How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are
generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the
safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries
the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C
that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not
translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's.

## 1. Layout

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml            the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency
├── build.rs              builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request
├── c/                    the C that remains, built into the crate
├── sys/<link-unit>/      one link unit's bindings
│   ├── wrapper.h         the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of
│   ├── allowlist.txt     one `function|type|var <regex>` per line, filled by the batches
│   ├── external.txt      the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line
│   ├── shims.h
│   ├── shims.c           the `crustify_<NAME>` macro shims
│   ├── bindings.rs       generated, committed
│   └── static_fns.c      generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed
└── src/sys.rs            the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own
```

Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its
own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode.

Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::<link_unit>` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw
binding is `sys::<name>`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it.
The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through
it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them.

`c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign
the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of
the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the
remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C
names, as the conventions' Exports section describes.

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

- the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the
  toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build
  regenerates the bytes a stable one committed;
- enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which
  the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums
  section describes;
- `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated;
- C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they
  hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt
  one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build
  uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script
  writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under
  `cfg(doctest)`;
- each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `<name>__extern`, in
  `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through
  `#[link_name = "<name>__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is:
  bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`;
- macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and
- an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and
  `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files.

An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline`
functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include
dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its
generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source
dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that
differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every
mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant.

A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it,
and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one
Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is
re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's
Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile
on any other, naming it.

The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of
the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks:
a generated header, force-included in every compile of that C and of its shims and
wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify_<library>_<name>`,
and bindgen binds each item under its C name with the prefixed symbol as its `link_name`,
so that the Rust names stay C's. The crate passes the header's path to the C builds of the
crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and
those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy.

The LLVM that generates the bindings, its libclang and the clang bindgen asks for the
system include dirs, is pinned with the bindgen version: its install prefix and version, in
the workspace manifest's `[workspace.metadata.crustify]`, as `bindgen-llvm` and
`bindgen-llvm-version`. Campaign mode generates with it
whatever drives the build, a sanitizer's or Miri's cargo driver included, which may name
another libclang of its own, and fails, naming both versions, when the pinned one is
missing or reports another version. A dependent's regeneration into `OUT_DIR`, compared
with nothing, takes the LLVM its host finds.

## 3. Build modes

The build script runs in one of four modes:

| mode | when | C |
|---|---|---|
| bundled | by default, but for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | `c/`, built statically into `OUT_DIR` by the target's own build system, in the configuration of the `plain` variant |
| shared | the `shared` feature | `c/`, built as shared libraries into `OUT_DIR`, the same way |
| system | the `system` feature, and by default for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | an install, found through `<LIB>_DIR`, then `pkg-config` |
| campaign | `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` names a variant, or `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` a private build | the variant's build, recorded in `crustify/artifacts/build.json`: its static archive, when it records one, else its shared libraries |

The campaign's repository sets `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` to `plain` in its
`.cargo/config.toml`, so that every build there runs in campaign mode unless the variable
names another variant, or is set empty to build as a dependent would.

In every mode, `shims.c` and `static_fns.c` are compiled against the headers the bindings
match, with the instrumentation of the C they link, and the bindings are the committed
ones unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates them into `OUT_DIR` from the headers of that
C. Campaign mode's tests and gates always regenerate them.

Bundled mode links the C statically, so that the bindings and the C they call always come
from the same revision; it sets no rpath. It builds `c/` against the out-of-tree libraries
its configuration uses as the target's build system finds them on the building host; a
dependent whose host lacks one supplies it through that build system's own search paths,
such as `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`. Shared mode leaves the remaining C's references
to ported modules undefined in its shared libraries, and the build script has the final
binary export what resolves them (`-Wl,--export-dynamic-symbol=<name>` for each export),
as a cdylib already does; the libraries are found beside the binary, through an `$ORIGIN`
rpath, and ship with it.

System mode serves a crate whose `c/` is still the whole source: once a port campaign has
switched a module, an install of the library would hold that module's C beside the Rust
that replaces it, and the build fails, naming the switched modules. It checks the
version: the library found must be the one the bindings were generated from, as its build
system reports it (`pkg-config --modversion`), or, for an out-of-tree library's wrapper, a
release ABI-compatible with it, which shares its soname. Another version fails the build
with both versions named, unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates the bindings for it. Each link
unit's module exports the version the bindings match as `C_VERSION`. `<LIB>_DIR` names an
install prefix: the build reads the headers under its `include/`, links the library under
its `lib/`, and takes the version from `lib/pkgconfig/<lib>.pc`. Without it, `pkg-config`
finds the library, which is linked as `pkg-config` resolves it, with no rpath.

An install carries neither the internal headers nor the functions its shared library does
not export, whichever header declares them, public or internal, and the shared libraries
shared mode builds lack the same functions, since the target's own configuration builds
them. Once the bindings reach either, system mode cannot serve the crate, nor shared mode
once they reach a function a shared library hides: the build fails in each, naming what
the library lacks, as system mode fails for a switched module, and bundled mode, whose
build in `OUT_DIR` has both, becomes the crate's default. The `bindgen` feature then regenerates from that build's
headers, never from an install's.

A link unit the target links as an executable, such as a command-line tool, has no
library. Bundled mode compiles its translation units as the target's build system records
them, without linking the executable, archives their objects and links the archive;
campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as
[`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system
modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive
member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references
the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member
that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That
unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which
reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested
through the variant's executable, run as a child process.

Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist
entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe
crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen`
feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from
the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's
documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it.
The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the
build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case
they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built,
so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that
records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section

the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the
remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records
none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export
what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does.

No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that
replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links
from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds
section describes.

## 4. Extending
## 5. Landing

A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the
bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match
their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

## 6. Publishing

The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate
holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the
C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the
package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

[dependencies]
# By path, not by Git: trybuild replaces only the paths of dependencies declared by path
# with `$FFIBOX` in compile-fail snapshots. By the canonical path of the campaign's own
# checkout of ffibox, the worktree of its working branch, `libgit2-crustify/devel`, so that
# the crate builds against the ffibox the campaign has changed, not against `devel`'s, which
# /crustify-rs/ffibox and the /opt/venv/share/ffibox link hold. Canonical, since trybuild
# replaces the canonicalized path while rustc prints the path as declared: a path through a
# link leaves the snapshots' paths absolute. glibc-bindings takes it by Git, which the [patch] below points at this path,
# so the graph holds one ffibox.
ffibox = { version = "0.1.1", path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox.libgit2-crustify" }
# libc's wrapper, the crustify-rs/glibc-crustify side campaign: pinned to a commit
# (`wrapper.pin` in crustify/artifacts/dependencies.json), and patched below to its clone
# beside this repository while the campaign extends it, by absolute path, which the batch
# worktrees under crustify/.worktrees resolve too.
glibc-bindings = { version = "0.1.0", git = "https://github.com/crustify-rs/glibc-crustify", rev = "24da93fc31a1788e73443cf4333d5037435d2d3f" }
pcre2-sys = "0.2"
nix = { version = "0.31.3", features = ["fs", "socket", "net", "poll", "process", "user", "feature", "signal", "mman", "time", "uio", "dir", "hostname"] }
flate2 = "1.1.11"
sha2 = "0.11.1"
hmac = "0.13.0"
md-5 = "0.11.0"
md4 = "0.11.0"
des = "0.9.0"
getrandom = "0.4.3"
rustls = "0.23.46"
rustls-webpki = "0.103.16"
pcre2 = "0.2.11"

[build-dependencies]
# Pinned exactly: the committed bindings are its output.
bindgen = { version = "=0.73.2", optional = true }
cc = "1.2"
pkg-config = "0.3"
serde_json = "1"

[dev-dependencies]
# The campaign's tests and gates regenerate the bindings, and check them against the
# committed ones; the crate's dependents build from the committed bindings.
libgit2-crustify = { path = ".", features = ["bindgen"] }
trybuild = "1.0"

[lints]
workspace = true

name = "ub_safe"
path = "tests/ub_safe/main.rs"

path = "tests/ub_unsafe/main.rs"

path = "tests/equiv/main.rs"

members = ["."]

---
name: soundness
description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."
---

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,

name: testing-builds
description: "The builds tests run against and how coverage is measured: the prebuilt variants, private builds, coverage instrumentation, objects, suites and figures, and a worklist's coverage. Read before building or choosing a test build, and before measuring or comparing coverage."

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

lines: //! `src/util/ctype_compat.h`: the locale-independent character classes libgit2 names
+//! The header has no translation unit and no state: its eight items are native Rust, reached

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done

273:## 6. Identity
## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.
## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

## 4. Cost and time
### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

#!/bin/bash
# run.sh <repo> <package> <cov dir>: build a coverage-instrumented scratch copy of the safe
# crate against the `coverage` variant, its test items under #[coverage(off)], and run each
# suite alone into <cov dir>/prof/<suite>: lib, each integration test binary, and doc. Each
# binary links the variant's C statically, so its profiles count the C and the Rust alike.
# report.py then reads the figures (testing spec, Coverage), with the variant's static archive
# as the C object.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' "$repo/Cargo.toml")
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree/crustify" "$out/prof"
(cd "$repo" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./crustify --exclude=./c --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
ln -s "$repo/c" "$tree/c"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/artifacts" "$tree/crustify/artifacts"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/builds" "$tree/crustify/builds"
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$tree/src" "$tree/src/lib.rs"
cd "$tree"
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=coverage CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")
  mkdir -p "$out/prof/$suite"
  echo "== $suite"
  LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/$suite/%p-%m.profraw" "$exe" --skip compile_fail > "$out/$suite.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in $suite"
  tail -3 "$out/$suite.log"
  "$exe" --list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ': test$' > "$out/$suite.count" || true
done < "$out/bins.txt"
mkdir -p "$out/prof/doc"
echo "== doc"
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/doc/%p-%m.profraw" cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --doc > "$out/doc.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in doc"
tail -3 "$out/doc.log"

"""report.py <cov dir> <name>=<dir>[:<dir>...][@<compilation dir>],... --c <C object>...

Merges each suite's profiles under <cov dir>/prof/, the four suites' union as TOTAL and every
suite's as ALL, and prints the TOTAL line of `llvm-cov report` for each named scope, with the C
objects and every test and doctest binary as objects for every suite. A scope's @<dir>
resolves the relative paths a C build recorded. MERGED=1 reuses the merged profiles, and ONLY=<suite> reports that one alone.

A scope written `<name>=@c`, such as `C=@c`, reads the C objects alone, with no source filter:
the archive holds only the link unit's TUs, whatever paths their build recorded. Any other
scope fails when a file it reports lies outside its dirs: llvm-cov falls back to every object
when its filters match no source, which would count the test binaries' std and Rust as C.

The C objects are those of the coverage variant's static archive, its `static` in build.json
(crustify/builds/coverage/crustify/libcrustify.a), which the test binaries link: each binary holds
only the TUs it reaches, so the archive, which llvm-cov reads member by member, gives every TU
its place in the denominator, one no test reaches at zero."""
import subprocess,sys,pathlib,json,glob,os
out0=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
nightly=os.environ.get("NIGHTLY") or next(l.split('"')[1] for l in open(out0/"tree"/"Cargo.toml") if l.startswith("nightly = "))
sysroot=subprocess.run(['rustc','+'+nightly,'--print','sysroot'],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
B=sysroot+'/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/'
out=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); scopes=dict(s.split('=',1) for s in sys.argv[2].split(','))
cobjs=sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--c')+1:]
bins=[l.split()[2] for l in (out/'bins.txt').read_text().splitlines()]
docs=[p for p in glob.glob(str(out/'doctests'/'**'/'rust_out'),recursive=True)]
objs=cobjs+bins+docs
suites=sorted(p.name for p in (out/'prof').iterdir() if any(p.glob('*.profraw')))
def merge(name,dirs):
    raws=[str(r) for d in dirs for r in (out/'prof'/d).glob('*.profraw')]
    prof=out/f'{name}.profdata'
    subprocess.run([B+'llvm-profdata','merge','-sparse','-o',str(prof)]+raws,check=True)
    return prof
def total(prof,srcs):
    cd=[]
    if srcs==['@c']: use,srcs=cobjs,[]
    else:
        use=objs
        if '@' in srcs[-1]: srcs[-1],c=srcs[-1].split('@'); cd=['-compilation-dir='+c]
    args=[B+'llvm-cov','report','-instr-profile',str(prof)]+cd+[use[0]]+sum((['-object',o] for o in use[1:]),[])+srcs
    r=subprocess.run(args,capture_output=True,text=True)
    if r.returncode: sys.exit(r.stderr[-2000:])
    lines=r.stdout.splitlines()
    if srcs and not cd:
        roots=[str(pathlib.Path(d).resolve()) for d in srcs]
        rows=[l.split()[0] for l in lines[2:] if l.strip() and not l.startswith(('-','TOTAL','Filename'))]
        stray=[f for f in rows if not any(str(pathlib.Path(f).resolve()).startswith(r+'/') or str(pathlib.Path(f).resolve())==r for r in roots)]
        if stray: sys.exit(f'scope {srcs} reports {len(stray)} files outside it, such as {stray[0]}: its filters match no source')
    t=[l for l in lines if l.startswith('TOTAL')][-1].split()
    # TOTAL regions missed cover functions missed exec lines missed cover branches missed cover
    return dict(lines=(int(t[7])-int(t[8]),int(t[7]),t[9]),functions=(int(t[4])-int(t[5]),int(t[4]),t[6]),regions=(int(t[1])-int(t[2]),int(t[1]),t[3]))
res={}
skip=os.environ.get('MERGED')
four=[x for x in suites if x!='doc']
only=os.environ.get('ONLY')
for s in ([only] if only else suites+['TOTAL','ALL']):
    prof=out/f'{s}.profdata' if skip else merge(s,four if s=='TOTAL' else suites if s=='ALL' else [s])
    res[s]={n:total(prof,src.split(':')) for n,src in scopes.items()}
    print(s,json.dumps(res[s]))
(out/(f'figures-{only}.json' if only else 'figures.json')).write_text(json.dumps(res,indent=1))

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---
# ffimap
ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.
It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:
```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```
Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:
```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```
Raw bindings that are a module of the crate, not a crate of their own, laid out and
generated as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, are named to `--sys-crates`
by their path, `crate::<path>`, beside the `-sys` crates that remain. A named module joins
the inventory and leaves every other counter, as a `-sys` crate does. Left unnamed, its C
types and functions are in no inventory, the cells that read it are taken over the other
crates' alone, and the generated code counts as the crate's own, all with no error. A module

    def env(self, stage: str, **extra: str) -> dict[str, str]:
        env = dict(os.environ)
        if stage == "miri":
            # Miri's builds kept apart from the variants', in the snapshot's target dir.
            env.setdefault("CARGO_TARGET_DIR", str(self.snap / "target" / "miri"))
        env.update(self.stage_env.get(stage, {}))
        env.update(extra)
        return env

    def cargo(self, stage: str) -> list[str]:
        """The command that runs cargo for `stage`, up to its subcommand."""
        if stage == "miri":
            return ["cargo", f"+{self.a.nightly}", "miri"]
        if stage == "lint":
            # The lints read no build of the C's but the bindings', which every variant
            # links alike: plain's.
            return [*self.runner, "plain"]
        return [*self.runner, stage]

    def run(self, stage: str, name: str, cmd: list[str], env: dict[str, str],
            timeout: int | None = None) -> dict:
        log = self.logs / f"{name}.log"
        start = time.monotonic()
        timed_out = False
        with open(log, "w") as out:
            out.write(f"$ {shlex.join(cmd)}\n")

            proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, cwd=self.snap, env=env, stdout=out,

            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                timed_out = True
                os.killpg(proc.pid, 9)
                rc = proc.wait()
        text = log.read_text(errors="replace")

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

# A macro's configured branches are compared over the arguments its Rust form takes

Status: `open`.

Goal: Idiomatic Rust, and Least constraint: the shim the rule keeps for branches that differ
would bind libc where the Rust form can state the one result its callers receive.

## Signal

A landed row's recurrence signal: `config-branches-of-one-result` (crustify `769d102`),
"a task message or plan correction that settles again whether a configuration-dependent
macro is ported or shimmed". `wave-220/batch-0/run-1`'s task message settled it again:
"Where the header has several configured branches, port what this build defines, as
`porting-symbols`' Macros section and `strnlen_h.rs` do."

## Evidence

`wave-220/batch-0/run-1` ported `src/util/ctype_compat.h`'s eight macros, `git__isalnum`,
`git__isalpha`, `git__isdigit`, `git__isprint`, `git__isspace`, `git__isxdigit`,
`git__tolower` and `git__toupper`. The header has two branches:

- this build's: `# define git__tolower(a) tolower((unsigned char)(a))`, and
  `(!!isalpha((unsigned char)(a)))` for each class, libc's `<ctype.h>`; and
- `GIT_WIN32`'s: `GIT_INLINE` functions comparing the `int` with ASCII ranges,
  `return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') ? (c + 32) : c;`.

`porting-symbols`' Macros section ports such a macro once "where every configuration's
expansion computes the same result for every input", and keeps the shim for one "whose
branches differ in what they compute". Read over the C's inputs, the `int` each macro
takes, these branches differ: `git__tolower(-1)` is `-1` under `GIT_WIN32` and `255`
elsewhere, `git__tolower(0x141)` is `0x141` and `'a'`. Read over the byte the expansion's own
cast leaves, the argument every other build classes, they agree for each of the 256: the
run checked it in glibc's `C`, `POSIX` and `C.UTF-8` locales against the `GIT_WIN32`
comparisons (a scratch C program, `crustify/tmp/w220b0/loc.c`, 0 bytes differing in each),
and the batch's equivalence tests compare the ports with glibc's functions for every `int`
from -300 to 600. The Rust form takes that byte, a `u8`, and its C callers' cast is
written where they call it, `c as u8`. Which reading the rule means, the rule does not say,
so the task message had to.

The process locale, which `<ctype.h>` reads and the Rust does not, is a second difference the
rule's "configuration" leaves open: it is no build configuration, but the state of an
out-of-tree library's entity, which `dependencies.json` already records in the entity's
`match` and note ("libgit2 runs in the C locale, where glibc's tables agree") and which its
route's confirmation checks.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Macros section.

## Change

In its second paragraph, replace "is ported once where every configuration's expansion
computes the same result for every input, and its documentation names the branches the
build does not take" with:

> is ported once where every configuration's expansion computes the same result for every
> input its Rust form takes: the arguments the expansion's own conversions leave, such as a
> cast to `unsigned char`, which its Rust callers make where they call it. Its documentation
> names the branches the build does not take, and the arguments outside that domain on
> which they part. The runtime state an out-of-tree entity of the expansion reads, such as
> the locale `<ctype.h>` follows, is no configuration: the entity's route and its
> confirmation settle it, as `dependencies`' Confirmation section describes.

## Validation

`wave-220/batch-0`'s port and tests, as the evidence describes: 11 `unit_pub` tests check
every byte against the C standard's C-locale classes, and 5 `equiv` tests compare the ports
with glibc's `<ctype.h>` for every `int` in -300..=600 and through three of the C's
expansion sites. A mutant `is_space` without the vertical tab fails three of them.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a configuration-dependent macro's branches are compared over the arguments its Rust form takes, after the expansion's own conversions; an out-of-tree entity's runtime state, such as the locale, is its route's, not a configuration | `libgit2-crustify`, `config-branches-over-the-rust-domain` | — | `config-branches-of-one-result`'s recurrence: a task message settled again whether `ctype_compat.h`'s macros, whose branches part only on `int`s outside a byte, are ported or shimmed | a task message or plan correction that settles again whether a configuration-dependent macro is ported or shimmed, or a review finding of a shim over branches that agree on the Rust form's domain | — |

## Review

None yet.

# API stability per C item `ffimap api` measures a promise a C-to-Rust migration makes to its Rust consumers: once a C item has a safe Rust API, wrapping it, porting it and its later stages leave that API alone. It reads the crate's rustdoc JSON, finds the Rust items that stand in for each C item through their anchors, and records their consumer-facing surface twice: raw, as the signatures stand, and as the **contract** a consumer may rely on whatever form a handle or an owner takes. Two such records, one at the item's first landing and one after a later landing, say whether the contract was kept, extended or changed. This document is what the two documents hold and every rule behind them. The scan's counters are [`schema.md`](schema.md)'s and have nothing to do with it. ## 1. Input ```sh cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc -p CRATE --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json (cd ffibox && cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc --lib -- -Z unstable-options \ --output-format json --document-private-items) ffimap api extract target/doc/CRATE.json --dep ffibox/target/doc/ffibox.json > before.json ``` `--dep` gives the rustdoc JSON of a crate the measured one depends on, and is repeatable. The contracts of handles and owners that are aliases into ffibox (`CBox`, `CArc`, `CVal`, …) need ffibox's, since the reborrows and trait impls those forms inherit live there; it is made with `--document-private-items` because the bounds rustdoc synthesises for ffibox's auto-trait impls name its private fields' types. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6 describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON format it reads. Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`. ## 2. C items and their stand-ins A C item is keyed by its anchor's `::`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`, `st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its own, exactly ``Wraps `::` `` or ``Replaces `::` ``, where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each. What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`: - `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks, or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing. - `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`, `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They are keyed as written. - `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out: rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers a search for it. ## 3. Locators and paths Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is matched with the next's: | item | locator | |---|---| | a free item | its canonical path | | an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` | | an item of a trait impl | `>::name` | | a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` | Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`. A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition into the parent changes nothing. An item of another crate is named by its definition's path in the `paths` table, `ffibox::refs::CBox` for instance, because this document does not record that crate's re-exports. Every type in a signature is rendered by its canonical path, never by what the source wrote, so an import or a reordering of the source gives the same bytes. A record's `paths` lists every public path the item is reached by, from the crate root through public modules and `pub use`, globs included. An associated item's are its owner's paths with its name appended. ## 4. Signatures Each stand-in's `sig` is normalised text by kind: - **functions and methods**: `decl` holds `const`, `async`, `unsafe`, the ABI, generics, the receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&'a mut self`, `self: Box`), the parameter types and return type, and where-clauses. A method also has the `impl` header it is declared in, generics and trait included, and a trait's method has `default`, whether it has a body. Parameter names are left out. - **structs, enums and unions**: `decl` holds the generics, the shape (`;`, `(n)`, `{}`) and `#[non_exhaustive]`. `fields` maps each public field to its type, and `variants` each variant to its shape and discriminant. `stripped` says whether rustdoc hid private fields or variants. `impls` maps the header of every trait impl rustdoc records for the type to its items (those it defines and the trait's provided ones it inherits) and its associated types and constants; the auto-trait impls rustdoc synthesises (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and `Freeze` and `UnsafeUnpin` where the nightly records them), negative ones as `!Send`, are included, and blanket impls are not, since they follow from the type's other impls. `members` holds the items of its inherent impls that stand in for no C item, each with its impl header. - **traits**: `decl` with generics, supertraits and `unsafe`; `required` and `provided` items, each with its declaration; `dyn_compatible`. - **type aliases**: `decl` holds the whole target, `type = ffibox::refs::CBox<…>`. - **constants and statics**: type and value; **associated constants and types**: their declaration and, in an impl, its header; **variants** and **fields**: their shape or type; a `macro_rules!` macro only its kind, since its body is not an interface. A trait impl's methods are recorded by name only: their signatures are the trait's, recorded where the trait is. ## 5. Handles and owners The types a consumer reaches a C type through -- `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal` and a policy type such as `FooFree` -- are not always annotated. An unannotated public struct, enum, union or trait of the crate is **associated** with C items by rule 1, else by rule 2, and a type alias by rule 3; `via` says which rule tied it: 1. `assoc_type`: a trait impl of the type sets an associated type to an anchored type, or a trait impl of an anchored type sets one to it. `impl CRefSeam for MailmapRef { type Cell = Mailmap; }` and `impl CCell for Mailmap { type Ref<'a> = MailmapRef<'a>; }` both tie `MailmapRef` to `st::git_mailmap`. 2. `owner`: the type's impls, or the trait's declaration, hold stand-ins; it is associated with their C items. A policy type whose `CDrop::c_drop` wraps `fn::git_mailmap_free` goes with that item. 3. `alias`: a type alias whose target names an anchored type, by id anywhere in the target, goes with that type's C items: `MailmapBox = CBox` with `st::git_mailmap`. A target naming none goes with the items of the types it names that rules 1 and 2 associated. An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. The **contract** of a type is that, and it, not the raw record, decides a C item's status. Every C item has a `contract` view: one entry per stand-in or associated item. - **A type** (`Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal`, a policy type, an enum) has its contract under its locator: - `generics`: how many lifetimes, types and constants it takes; - `fields` (public ones), `shape` (only when a consumer can build it, no field hidden), `variants` and `non_exhaustive`; - `methods`: every method a consumer can call on it, by name, over every route: on the form itself, through its dereferences (`&self` methods through `Deref`, `&mut self` ones too through `DerefMut`) and on what its reborrows return. The route is not recorded, and the first found names a method; - `reborrows`: what `as_ref` and `as_mut` return. One returning the form's own type adds nothing and is left out; - `traits`: the traits it implements that a consumer can use, with their arguments; - `derefs`: targets reached through a dereference that the contract does not look inside (a slice, `str`, a primitive, a standard type), whose methods are the standard library's. - **A method of a handle or owner** is keyed `method::`, without its owner, since a port moves it from `FooRef` to `impl Foo`, and holds its normalised signatures. - **Any other function** has its normalised signature; anything else its raw record. Signatures in a contract are normalised so that each form reads the same: a type equal to the target of one of the crate's public aliases is written as the alias, so `&'a Foo` reads `FooRef<'_>` once `FooRef<'a> = &'a Foo`; lifetimes are erased; `Self` is the type the method is called on; a projection such as `::Ref<'_>` is resolved through `Foo`'s impl; parameter names are dropped; and a `self` receiver of a `Copy` type is `&self`. **What is no part of a contract:** | left out | why | |---|---| | functions without a `self` receiver | reached through a type path, which a change of form changes | | the seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr`, `from_void_ptr`, `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `from_c`, `into_c`, `as_c_ptr`, `from_raw`, `as_object` | the conversion between a wrapper and its raw form, ffimap's seam list | | a method with a raw pointer or `NonNull` in its signature | raw access | | `unsafe` methods | they exist because a form wraps C; an anchored one is its own C item's | | anchored methods | each is its own C item's stand-in, compared there | | every method of a plumbing crate's type (`--plumbing`, ffibox by default) but `as_ref` and `as_mut` | what one form offers beyond the native ones, such as `try_clone` or `policy` | | the traits of a plumbing crate (`CCell`, `CDrop`, `CRefSeam`, …) | plumbing | | `Drop`, `StructuralPartialEq`, `Freeze`, `UnsafeUnpin` | no consumer can use them | | `Pointer` | it formats the address: raw access | | `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `AsRef`, `AsMut`, `Borrow`, `BorrowMut` | recorded as dereferences and reborrows, and through the methods they reach | | blanket impls | they follow from the others | **Where a form's surface comes from.** A type of the crate, or of a crate given with `--dep`, answers from its impls in that crate's JSON: an impl applies when its self type matches the form, and its bounds are checked against the impl lists rustdoc records (which list the blanket impls that apply), so `impl Send for CBox` holds for `CBox` exactly when `Foo` and `FooFree` are `Send`. A standard pointer form answers from a fixed model: `&T` and `&mut T` dereference to `T`, `Box` too, with `as_ref`/`as_mut`, `Arc` and `Rc` shared, `Pin

` as `P`, and each implements `Clone`, `Copy`, `Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, `Default`, `Debug`, `Display`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash` under the standard library's conditions on `T`; `NonNull` and `PhantomData` are modelled for the bounds they appear in. **Unresolved.** A contract that needs what is not there -- a type of a crate whose JSON was not given, a standard type the model does not cover, a bound that cannot be decided, such as one on the free parameter of a generic alias -- lists it under `unresolved`, and that entry is compared on its raw record instead (section 10). `contract_missing_deps` names the crates whose JSON would have resolved more. ## 7. The unattributed surface A public item of the crate that is neither a stand-in nor associated is **unattributed**. It is recorded by the Rust module of its canonical path, under `unattributed`, with the same records, and compared the same way, so a change to it is reported though no C item owns it. ## 8. Coverage `coverage` counts how far the anchors reach. `public` counts the crate's reachable items by role: free items by kind, `inherent_item` and `trait_impl_item` for the items of a type's impls (blanket and synthesised impls aside), `trait_item`, `variant` and `field`. `anchored` counts those that carry an anchor. `c_items` and `c_items_by_kind` count the keys, `stand_ins` the records, `associated` and `unattributed` the items those sections hold. ## 9. The extract ```json { "api": 2, "source": {"crate": "libgit2", "crate_version": "0.1.0", "format_version": 61, "deps": ["ffibox"], "plumbing": ["ffibox"]}, "items": { "st::git_mailmap": { "anchor": "Wraps", "stand_ins": {"libgit2::…::Mailmap": {"anchor": "Wraps", "kind": "struct", "paths": ["libgit2::…::Mailmap"], "sig": {…}}}, "associated": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type_alias", "via": ["alias"], "paths": […], "sig": {…}}}, "contract": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type", "generics": {…}, "methods": {…}, "reborrows": {…}, "traits": […]}, …} } }, "contract_missing_deps": [], "unattributed": {"libgit2::…::odb": {"libgit2::…::OdbDataStrVec": {…}}}, "anchors": {"malformed": [], "unknown_kinds": {}, "without_alias": []}, "coverage": {…} } ``` An item's `anchor` is its stand-ins' verb, or `mixed` when they differ. `api` is the extract's own version, bumped when a rule or the shape changes, and two extracts of different versions are not compared. Keys are sorted and the JSON is indented by one, so one document gives one byte sequence. ## 10. The diff `ffimap api diff BEFORE AFTER` takes two extracts, or two rustdoc JSON documents it extracts first (with the same `--dep` and `--plumbing`), and classifies every C item by its contract view: | status | when | |---|---| | `kept` | every entry is identical | | `extended` | only additions | | `changed` | anything lost or rewritten | | `removed` | the key is gone | | `new` | the key first appears | In the contract view an entry gained, a method, a reborrow, a trait, a dereference target, a signature beside a method's others, a field of a type with hidden fields or a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is an addition; an entry, a method, a reborrow, a trait or a signature lost or rewritten, a generics count changed, and a field or variant gained where a consumer could build or match every one, is a change. A type whose raw record moved while its contract did not is a **retarget**: the item records `retarget` with the raw declarations before and after, and stays kept. `raw_status` says when the raw view would have classified the item otherwise. `--raw` classifies by the raw records instead, and an unresolved contract entry is compared on its raw record; the raw rules, where an addition and a change are: | addition (`extended`) | change (`changed`) | |---|---| | a stand-in or an associated item | a stand-in or an associated item lost, or its kind changed | | a public path | a public path lost | | a trait impl, auto traits included | a trait impl lost, auto traits included (`Send` becoming `!Send` is both) | | an item or associated type in a trait impl | one lost, or an associated type retargeted | | an inherent member no anchor claims | a member lost or rewritten | | a provided trait item, or a required one made provided | a required trait item, or any trait item lost or rewritten | | a field of a struct with private fields | a field of one without, or any field lost or retyped | | a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum | a variant of an exhaustive enum, or any variant lost or rewritten | | | a `decl` or `impl` header rewritten: a signature, an alias target, a constant's value | An item whose anchor verb moved records it as `anchor: {before, after}`, and `anchor_moves` counts the moves, so a wrap-to-port step reads `Wraps->Replaces` whatever the status. A key gone and a key come with the same path, one of each, are one C item whose anchor kind was relabelled: it is compared as one and records `rekeyed` with its old key. The JSON form, the default, holds the `view` that decided, `totals`, `anchor_moves`, `rekeyed`, `retargeted`, `unresolved`, every C item's `status` with its `changes`, `raw_status`, `retarget` and `unresolved`, and `unattributed` with its own totals by module, always on raw records. Each change names the entry's locator, the `part` that moved (`method`, `trait`, `reborrow`, `decl`, `impl`, `member`, `path`, …), whether it was `added`, `removed` or `changed`, its `severity` (`extended` or `changed`), the values before and after, and `view: raw` when an unresolved entry was compared raw. `--format text` prints the items that are neither kept nor new, with one line per change, then the totals. `--items` restricts the C items to a list of keys, a batch's worklist, and lists those found in neither document under `missing`. The unattributed surface is reported whatever it holds, since no worklist names it. ## 11. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen.
